questions.question: What is @RestController in Spring Boot?
questions.title: @RestController annotation explained
questions.direct_answer: `@RestController` is a convenience annotation that combines `@Controller` and `@ResponseBody`. Spring MVC treats the class as a controller and writes each handler's return value to the HTTP response body through a compatible `HttpMessageConverter`.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `@RestController` combines `@Controller` with class-wide `@ResponseBody` behavior.
Request-mapping annotations still decide which handler method receives the request.
A handler return value is written to the response body instead of being used for view rendering.
A compatible `HttpMessageConverter` chooses how to write the body; JSON is common when Jackson is configured.
The annotation does not choose the status code, validate input, or guarantee that every response is JSON.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`@RestController` is Spring MVC's convenience annotation for controllers whose handler results normally belong in the HTTP response body. It is itself annotated with `@Controller` and `@ResponseBody`, so Spring discovers the class as a controller and applies response-body handling to all of its mapped methods.

For a request such as `GET /orders/42`, `@GetMapping` selects the Java method. If that method returns an `OrderView`, Spring passes the value to an `HttpMessageConverter`. With Jackson available and JSON selected through content negotiation, the object becomes a JSON response such as `{"id":42,"item":"Keyboard"}`.

`@RestController` does not perform JSON conversion by itself. The Java return type, configured converters, the mapping's `produces` condition, and the client's `Accept` header help select the representation. A returned `String` is normally handled by `StringHttpMessageConverter`; it is not automatically quoted as JSON.

I use `@RestController` for HTTP APIs and `@Controller` for controllers that mainly return view names and models. A regular `@Controller` method can still return response data by adding `@ResponseBody` to that method. Status selection, request-body binding, validation, and exception handling remain separate concerns.

beats.stage: A controller whose results become response bodies
beats.spokenText: `@RestController` is Spring MVC's convenience annotation for controllers whose handler results normally belong in the HTTP response body. beats.recallRule: @RestController supplies controller discovery plus response-body handling; a message converter writes the actual representation.

sections.title: How a controller return value becomes an HTTP body
sections.content:
`@Controller` is a Spring component stereotype for the web layer. `@RestController` includes that stereotype, so normal component scanning can register the class and Spring MVC can inspect its `@RequestMapping`, `@GetMapping`, and other handler methods.

After a request is mapped and the handler returns, `@ResponseBody` changes how Spring interprets the result. Instead of treating the result as view information, Spring uses response-body processing and asks its message converters whether they can write that Java type for the selected media type.

Spring Boot's web starter normally configures Jackson when it is on the classpath. A record or DTO can then be written as JSON. That common setup explains why `@RestController` is closely associated with JSON, but XML, text, byte arrays, files, and custom formats can use different converters.

The return type still matters. A Java `String` is normally written by `StringHttpMessageConverter` as text. A DTO can use the Jackson converter for JSON. If the client requests a representation that none of the configured converters can write, the request can end with `406 Not Acceptable` rather than silently becoming JSON.

The annotation affects handler return values only. Incoming JSON needs `@RequestBody`; constraints need a validation trigger such as `@Valid`; a creation response still needs a suitable status such as `201`; and exceptions still need framework or application mappings. Keeping these jobs separate makes controller behavior predictable.

sections.title: From mapped handler to response body
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
  A[GET /orders/42] --> B[DispatcherServlet selects handler]
  B --> C[Controller returns OrderView]
  C --> D[HttpMessageConverter writes value]
  D --> E[200 response with JSON body]
```

questions.question: What is the difference between @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping?
questions.title: HTTP method mapping annotations in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: The difference between `@GetMapping`, `@PostMapping`, `@PutMapping`, and `@DeleteMapping` is the HTTP method each one maps: GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE respectively. All four are composed `@RequestMapping` shortcuts; they control routing, while the controller code must honor each method's HTTP meaning.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `@GetMapping` selects GET requests, which have safe and idempotent semantics.
`@PostMapping` selects POST requests for resource-specific processing; POST is not idempotent by default.
`@PutMapping` selects PUT requests that create or replace state at the target URI; PUT is idempotent.
`@DeleteMapping` selects DELETE requests that remove the target resource's current association; DELETE is idempotent.
Spring enforces the route and mapping conditions, not the safety or idempotency of the code inside the method.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`@GetMapping`, `@PostMapping`, `@PutMapping`, and `@DeleteMapping` are method-specific forms of `@RequestMapping`. They tell Spring MVC which Java handler is eligible for a GET, POST, PUT, or DELETE request and can also declare path, header, parameter, `consumes`, and `produces` conditions.

GET asks for a current representation and has safe, idempotent semantics. POST asks the target resource to process the request content, so it is often used to create a server-named resource but is not limited to creation. POST is not idempotent by default.

PUT sends state for a known target URI and asks the server to create or replace that resource state. DELETE asks the server to remove the target resource's current association. PUT and DELETE are idempotent: repeating the same request has the same intended effect, although the later response can differ.

The annotation does not make an implementation correct. A `@GetMapping` method can still wrongly update a database, and a `@PutMapping` method can still trigger duplicate side effects. I choose the mapping from the HTTP contract, implement its semantics in the service, and test method, path, status, headers, and body together.

beats.stage: Each annotation selects one HTTP method
beats.spokenText: `@GetMapping`, `@PostMapping`, `@PutMapping`, and `@DeleteMapping` are method-specific forms of `@RequestMapping`. They tell Spring MVC which Java handler is eligible for a GET, POST, PUT, or DELETE request and can also declare path, header, parameter, `consumes`, and `produces` conditions.

beats.stage: Retrieve a representation or process content
beats.spokenText: GET asks for a current representation and has safe, idempotent semantics. POST asks the target resource to process the request content, so it is often used to create a server-named resource but is not limited to creation. POST is not idempotent by default.

beats.stage: Replace known state or remove an association
beats.spokenText: PUT sends state for a known target URI and asks the server to create or replace that resource state. DELETE asks the server to remove the target resource's current association. PUT and DELETE are idempotent: repeating the same request has the same intended effect, although the later response can differ.

beats.stage: Annotations route; application code preserves semantics
beats.spokenText: The annotation does not make an implementation correct. A `@GetMapping` method can still wrongly update a database, and a `@PutMapping` method can still trigger duplicate side effects. I choose the mapping from the HTTP contract, implement its semantics in the service, and test method, path, status, headers, and body together.
beats.recallRule: GET retrieves, POST processes, PUT creates or replaces a known target, and DELETE removes its association; Spring only maps the request.

sections.title: Method mappings express the operation's HTTP contract
sections.content:
Each of the four annotations is meta-annotated with `@RequestMapping` and fixes the HTTP method condition. `@GetMapping("/{id}")`, for example, is the readable equivalent of a request mapping whose method is GET. A class-level mapping can provide the shared `/orders` path.

GET is safe because the client does not request a state change. Logging and metrics may still happen, but a GET endpoint should not use a query such as `/orders/42?delete=true` to perform deletion. GET is also idempotent, which allows clients and intermediaries to reason about retrieval and retry behavior.

POST means resource-specific processing. Creating an order under `/orders` is a common example because the server chooses the new order URI, but POST can also submit a command or start a process. A retry can repeat the action unless the API adds its own idempotency design.

PUT targets a URI the client already knows. It asks to create or replace that resource's state, and an identical retry has the same intended effect. DELETE is also idempotent even when the first call returns `204` and a later call returns `404`; idempotency concerns the requested effect, not identical response messages.

Status codes depend on the outcome rather than the annotation alone. A successful POST creation often returns `201 Created` and a `Location`; a PUT can return `201` when it creates the target or `200`/`204` when it replaces it; a DELETE may return `204`. The route, service behavior, and response contract must agree.

sections.title: The four mappings and their HTTP meaning
sections.content:
| Annotation | Request meaning | Safe? | Idempotent? | Common order example |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| `@GetMapping` | Retrieve a current representation | Yes | Yes | `GET /orders/42` |
| `@PostMapping` | Let the target process request content | No | Not guaranteed | `POST /orders` |
| `@PutMapping` | Create or replace state at the target URI | No | Yes | `PUT /orders/42` |
| `@DeleteMapping` | Remove the target resource's current association | No | Yes | `DELETE /orders/42` |

questions.question: What is @RequestBody and how does it work?
questions.title: @RequestBody in Spring Boot REST controllers
questions.direct_answer: `@RequestBody` is the annotation that tells Spring MVC to read the HTTP request body and convert it to the declared Java parameter type through an `HttpMessageConverter`. The request `Content-Type` identifies the format, and `@Valid` can validate the converted object afterward.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `@RequestBody` binds the HTTP message body, not a path variable or query parameter.
Spring chooses a reader from the request `Content-Type` and the Java parameter type.
With Jackson configured, `application/json` can be converted to a record or DTO.
`@Valid` runs Bean Validation after conversion; `@RequestBody` alone does not validate constraints.
Malformed JSON, an unsupported media type, and a valid object with invalid fields fail at different stages.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`@RequestBody` binds the content of an HTTP request to a controller method parameter. Spring MVC looks at the request's `Content-Type` and the declared Java type, selects an `HttpMessageConverter`, reads the body, and passes the converted value to the handler.

For `Content-Type: application/json`, Jackson commonly converts `{"customerName":"Asha","quantity":2}` into a `CreateOrderRequest`. `Content-Type` describes what the client sent; the `Accept` header is separate and describes which response formats the client can accept.

Conversion and validation are different steps. `@RequestBody` creates the Java value. Adding `@Valid` causes Jakarta Validation constraints such as `@NotBlank` and `@Positive` to run on that value. A validation failure normally raises `MethodArgumentNotValidException` and becomes `400 Bad Request`.

Malformed JSON usually fails earlier with `HttpMessageNotReadableException`, while an unsupported request format or a `consumes` mismatch can produce `415 Unsupported Media Type`. The body is required by default. I use query parameters for small filters and HTML form fields, path variables for resource identity, and `@RequestBody` for a structured message body.

beats.stage: Request bytes become a Java parameter
beats.spokenText: `@RequestBody` binds the content of an HTTP request to a controller method parameter. Spring MVC looks at the request's `Content-Type` and the declared Java type, selects an `HttpMessageConverter`, reads the body, and passes the converted value to the handler.

beats.stage: Content-Type identifies the incoming format
beats.spokenText: For `Content-Type: application/json`, Jackson commonly converts `{"customerName":"Asha","quantity":2}` into a `CreateOrderRequest`. `Content-Type` describes what the client sent; the `Accept` header is separate and describes which response formats the client can accept.

beats.stage: @Valid checks the converted object
beats.spokenText: Conversion and validation are different steps. `@RequestBody` creates the Java value. Adding `@Valid` causes Jakarta Validation constraints such as `@NotBlank` and `@Positive` to run on that value. A validation failure normally raises `MethodArgumentNotValidException` and becomes `400 Bad Request`.

beats.stage: Bad syntax, wrong media type, and invalid fields differ
beats.spokenText: Malformed JSON usually fails earlier with `HttpMessageNotReadableException`, while an unsupported request format or a `consumes` mismatch can produce `415 Unsupported Media Type`. The body is required by default. I use query parameters for small filters and HTML form fields, path variables for resource identity, and `@RequestBody` for a structured message body.
beats.recallRule: Content-Type selects a converter, the converter creates the object, and @Valid checks that object.

sections.title: The request body passes through conversion before validation
sections.content:
An HTTP request body is a sequence of bytes with metadata. `Content-Type: application/json` tells Spring MVC to look for a message converter that can read JSON into the handler's declared parameter type. `@RequestBody` marks that parameter as the destination.

With Spring Boot's normal JSON setup, Jackson matches JSON properties to record components, constructor parameters, or bean properties. Conversion can fail before the controller runs if the JSON is malformed, a value has the wrong shape, or the chosen converter cannot create the requested Java type.

Bean Validation comes next. `@Valid` is the trigger that asks the configured validator to inspect constraints on the converted object. In the example, a blank customer name or a quantity below one produces a validation error even though the JSON syntax itself is correct.

These failures should not be merged conceptually. Malformed JSON generally becomes `400`; a rejected request media type becomes `415`; constraint violations on this request object generally become `400`. A global advice can give them one documented error format without pretending they have the same cause.

A GET request body has no generally defined HTTP semantics, so APIs should not depend on one for ordinary retrieval. Servlet form data is also better read through request parameters because form parsing and direct body access can conflict. `@RequestBody` is most natural for structured bodies on operations such as POST, PUT, or PATCH.

sections.title: The @RequestBody pipeline
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
  A[Body plus Content-Type] --> B[Message converter]
  B -->|readable| C[CreateOrderRequest]
  B -->|unreadable| F[400 response]
  C --> D[Validation with @Valid]
  D -->|valid| E[Controller method]
  D -->|invalid| F
```

questions.question: How do you return different HTTP status codes in Spring Boot?
questions.title: HTTP status codes in Spring Boot — ResponseEntity and @ResponseStatus
questions.direct_answer: Return `ResponseEntity` when status, headers, or body depend on the result; use `@ResponseStatus` when a handler has one fixed status; and map exceptions with `@ExceptionHandler` or `ResponseStatusException`. The status must describe the actual HTTP outcome.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `ResponseEntity<T>` carries a runtime status, response headers, and an optional body.
`@ResponseStatus` declares a fixed status on a handler or exception; it is runtime metadata, not compile-time behavior.
`@ExceptionHandler` or `ResponseStatusException` can translate a failure into an HTTP response.
A creation commonly returns `201 Created` with `Location`; `204 No Content` must not contain a body.
No mapping annotation forces one success status—choose from the endpoint's actual result.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Spring MVC offers several ways to set an HTTP status. `ResponseEntity` is the most flexible because the method builds the status, headers, and optional body for that execution. A lookup can therefore return `200 OK` with an order or `404 Not Found` when the order does not exist.

For a successful creation, `ResponseEntity.created(location).body(order)` produces `201 Created`, sets the `Location` header, and writes the representation. For a successful operation with nothing to return, `ResponseEntity.noContent().build()` produces `204 No Content` with no body.

`@ResponseStatus` is useful when one handler always has the same status, such as a delete method that always returns `204`. It can also annotate an exception, although that couples the exception type to HTTP. The annotation is applied at runtime; saying it is fixed at compile time is incorrect.

For failures, an `@ExceptionHandler` can create a safe `ResponseEntity` or `ProblemDetail`, and `ResponseStatusException` can carry a status from application code. I avoid the `reason` attribute of `@ResponseStatus` for REST APIs because it uses the Servlet error mechanism and can produce a container HTML page. The final code always comes from the real outcome, not simply from GET, POST, or DELETE.

beats.stage: ResponseEntity controls status, headers, and body
beats.spokenText: Spring MVC offers several ways to set an HTTP status. `ResponseEntity` is the most flexible because the method builds the status, headers, and optional body for that execution. A lookup can therefore return `200 OK` with an order or `404 Not Found` when the order does not exist.

beats.stage: 201 carries a new location; 204 carries no body
beats.spokenText: For a successful creation, `ResponseEntity.created(location).body(order)` produces `201 Created`, sets the `Location` header, and writes the representation. For a successful operation with nothing to return, `ResponseEntity.noContent().build()` produces `204 No Content` with no body.

beats.stage: @ResponseStatus supplies runtime response metadata
beats.spokenText: `@ResponseStatus` is useful when one handler always has the same status, such as a delete method that always returns `204`. It can also annotate an exception, although that couples the exception type to HTTP. The annotation is applied at runtime; saying it is fixed at compile time is incorrect.

beats.stage: Error mapping belongs at the web boundary
beats.spokenText: For failures, an `@ExceptionHandler` can create a safe `ResponseEntity` or `ProblemDetail`, and `ResponseStatusException` can carry a status from application code. I avoid the `reason` attribute of `@ResponseStatus` for REST APIs because it uses the Servlet error mechanism and can produce a container HTML page. The final code always comes from the real outcome, not simply from GET, POST, or DELETE.
beats.recallRule: Use ResponseEntity for a result-dependent response, @ResponseStatus for one fixed outcome, and exception mapping for failures.

sections.title: Status, headers, and body form one response contract
sections.content:
A normal response-body return value usually results in `200 OK`, but many endpoints need a different outcome. `ResponseEntity` represents the complete application-controlled response: its status code, headers, and body. Builders such as `ok`, `created`, `accepted`, `noContent`, and `notFound` make the intent readable.

A `201 Created` response says that processing created one or more resources. The primary new resource is identified by `Location`, or by the target URI when no `Location` is sent. When the server has the new URI, returning it helps the client find the resource without guessing.

`204 No Content` means the request succeeded and there is no response content. It cannot carry a body or trailers. If the API needs to return a deletion result or another representation, `200 OK` with that body is a clearer contract than attaching content to `204`.

`@ResponseStatus` declares a status on a controller method or exception class. It is concise for a stable outcome, but a `ResponseEntity` returned by the method can take precedence. Setting `reason` is different from setting only the code: it invokes `sendError`, completes the response, and commonly lets the Servlet container produce HTML, so it is a poor fit for a JSON API.

Exceptions need deliberate translation. A domain lookup does not become `404` merely because its exception name contains 'NotFound'. An exception handler, an annotated exception, or `ResponseStatusException` must define that mapping. The response should expose safe client information while retaining technical detail in server-side diagnostics.

sections.title: Choose the status mechanism from the outcome
sections.content:
| Need | Spring MVC choice | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Status varies by result | `ResponseEntity<T>` | `200` when found, `404` when missing |
| Status and headers are returned together | `ResponseEntity<T>` | `201` with `Location` |
| One handler always has the same status | `@ResponseStatus` | Fixed `204` after deletion |
| One exception needs an HTTP mapping | `@ExceptionHandler`, annotated exception, or `ResponseStatusException` | Domain missing order becomes `404` |
| Success has no response content | `ResponseEntity.noContent().build()` | Empty `204` response |

questions.question: What is @ControllerAdvice and how do you handle exceptions globally in Spring Boot?
questions.title: @ControllerAdvice for global exception handling
questions.direct_answer: `@ControllerAdvice` is a Spring component that shares `@ExceptionHandler`, `@InitBinder`, and `@ModelAttribute` methods across controllers. For REST APIs, `@RestControllerAdvice` adds response-body handling so an exception handler can return a safe `ProblemDetail` or DTO with the correct HTTP status.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `@ControllerAdvice` applies shared controller advice; `@RestControllerAdvice` also applies `@ResponseBody` semantics.
`@ExceptionHandler` maps a specific exception to a status, headers, and safe error body.
A controller-local handler is considered before a global advice handler.
`ProblemDetail` is Spring's RFC 9457 error representation and normally uses `application/problem+json` with Jackson.
Advice does not automatically handle every application or security exception, and a catch-all `Exception` handler is not mandatory.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`@ControllerAdvice` defines behavior shared across Spring MVC controllers. Its `@ExceptionHandler` methods can translate exceptions raised during controller processing into HTTP responses. `@RestControllerAdvice` combines that feature with `@ResponseBody`, so returned error values are written through message conversion instead of being treated as views.

For example, the service can throw `OrderNotFoundException`. A global handler for that exact type can create a `ProblemDetail` with status `404`, a safe explanation, and an application error code. Spring uses the problem status for the HTTP response and, with Jackson, favors `application/problem+json`.

Specific mappings keep the boundary clear: a validation failure can become `400`, a missing order can become `404`, and an unexpected failure can remain `500` without exposing a stack trace. For built-in Spring MVC exceptions, extending `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler` or enabling Boot's Problem Details support can provide a useful base.

A local `@ExceptionHandler` is checked before global advice. Multiple advice beans also have ordering and exception-match rules, so handlers should be specific and tested. Exceptions raised in a security filter may be handled by Spring Security before MVC, and asynchronous or background failures are outside controller advice. I add a catch-all only when the application has a clear logging and safe-response policy—not as a required ritual.

beats.stage: One exception mapping can serve many controllers
beats.spokenText: `@ControllerAdvice` defines behavior shared across Spring MVC controllers. Its `@ExceptionHandler` methods can translate exceptions raised during controller processing into HTTP responses. `@RestControllerAdvice` combines that feature with `@ResponseBody`, so returned error values are written through message conversion instead of being treated as views.

beats.stage: A domain exception becomes a safe HTTP problem
beats.spokenText: For example, the service can throw `OrderNotFoundException`. A global handler for that exact type can create a `ProblemDetail` with status `404`, a safe explanation, and an application error code. Spring uses the problem status for the HTTP response and, with Jackson, favors `application/problem+json`.

beats.stage: Different causes keep different statuses
beats.spokenText: Specific mappings keep the boundary clear: a validation failure can become `400`, a missing order can become `404`, and an unexpected failure can remain `500` without exposing a stack trace. For built-in Spring MVC exceptions, extending `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler` or enabling Boot's Problem Details support can provide a useful base.

beats.stage: Advice is global to selected controllers, not every failure
beats.spokenText: A local `@ExceptionHandler` is checked before global advice. Multiple advice beans also have ordering and exception-match rules, so handlers should be specific and tested. Exceptions raised in a security filter may be handled by Spring Security before MVC, and asynchronous or background failures are outside controller advice. I add a catch-all only when the application has a clear logging and safe-response policy—not as a required ritual.
beats.recallRule: Use specific advice handlers to translate controller exceptions into one safe HTTP error contract; do not treat advice as a universal exception net.

sections.title: Global advice translates controller failures at one web boundary
sections.content:
`@ControllerAdvice` is meta-annotated as a Spring component. When MVC starts, its infrastructure discovers advice beans and makes their `@ExceptionHandler`, `@InitBinder`, and `@ModelAttribute` methods available to controllers. Selectors can limit advice by package, annotation, or assignable controller type.

When a controller invocation raises an exception, Spring MVC uses its exception-resolver chain. An `@ExceptionHandler` can match the exception type and return the same kinds of response values as a controller method. A controller-local handler is considered before a global handler, which lets one controller deliberately override a shared rule.

`@RestControllerAdvice` is convenient for JSON APIs because it adds response-body semantics. Returning `ProblemDetail` gives the response the standard RFC 9457 fields such as `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, and `instance`. Spring also supports application-specific properties such as an error code.

Framework exceptions need their own plan. `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler` handles Spring MVC's `ErrorResponse` exceptions and is designed as a base class for advice. In Spring Boot 3.3.1, `spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true` enables auto-configured Problem Details handling for built-in MVC exceptions; application domain exceptions still need deliberate mappings.

Safe error content is different from diagnostic logging. A client may receive 'Order 99 was not found' and `ORDER_NOT_FOUND`, while the server retains a trace or correlation identifier. Raw SQL messages, filesystem paths, credentials, and stack traces must not be copied into the response.

Advice applies around MVC handler processing, not every thread in the process. Authentication and access-denied failures are commonly handled in Spring Security's filter chain, and background job failures need their own boundary. A broad `Exception.class` handler can also hide defects or interfere with another resolver, so it should exist only with a tested status, body, logging, and rethrow policy.

sections.title: How MVC selects a global exception handler
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
  A[Exception reaches MVC] --> B{Local handler?}
  B -->|yes| C[Local error response]
  B -->|no| D{Advice handler?}
  D -->|yes| E[ProblemDetail response]
  D -->|no| F[Next resolver]
```

questions.question: What is @RequestMapping at the class level used for?
questions.title: @RequestMapping class-level base path
questions.direct_answer: A class-level `@RequestMapping` is a declaration of request conditions shared by all handler methods in a controller—most commonly a base path. Method-level mappings add or narrow conditions to form each final endpoint.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A class-level path such as `/orders` is combined with method paths such as `/{id}`.
`@GetMapping`, `@PostMapping`, and the other method-specific annotations narrow the final route by HTTP method.
Class-level `produces`, `consumes`, header, or parameter conditions can describe shared controller rules.
Method-level `consumes` and `produces` replace, rather than extend, the corresponding class-level condition.
The annotation groups routes; it does not provide authorization, tenant checks, or automatic API compatibility.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A class-level `@RequestMapping` defines conditions shared by a controller's handler methods. The most common use is a base path. If the class maps `/orders` and a method has `@GetMapping("/{id}")`, Spring combines them into `GET /orders/{id}`.

The class mapping can also declare shared media types, headers, or request-parameter conditions. A method-specific mapping then adds its HTTP method and relative path. This avoids repeating the same resource prefix and makes the controller's public area visible in one place.

The combination is not identical for every attribute. Paths are combined, but a method-level `consumes` or `produces` condition overrides the class-level condition instead of adding to it. That matters when one endpoint accepts a different media type from the rest of the controller.

I keep the class mapping focused on conditions that truly apply to the whole resource. I do not use a bare method-level `@RequestMapping` when a method-specific annotation is clearer, and I do not place two request-mapping annotations on the same element. Changing a class base path changes every public route below it, so clients, tests, documentation, and gateway rules must move together.

beats.stage: Class and method paths form one endpoint
beats.spokenText: A class-level `@RequestMapping` defines conditions shared by a controller's handler methods. The most common use is a base path. If the class maps `/orders` and a method has `@GetMapping("/{id}")`, Spring combines them into `GET /orders/{id}`.

beats.stage: One controller can publish common media rules
beats.spokenText: The class mapping can also declare shared media types, headers, or request-parameter conditions. A method-specific mapping then adds its HTTP method and relative path. This avoids repeating the same resource prefix and makes the controller's public area visible in one place.

beats.stage: Media conditions can replace class-level values
beats.spokenText: The combination is not identical for every attribute. Paths are combined, but a method-level `consumes` or `produces` condition overrides the class-level condition instead of adding to it. That matters when one endpoint accepts a different media type from the rest of the controller.

beats.stage: A shared annotation changes every endpoint below it
beats.spokenText: I keep the class mapping focused on conditions that truly apply to the whole resource. I do not use a bare method-level `@RequestMapping` when a method-specific annotation is clearer, and I do not place two request-mapping annotations on the same element. Changing a class base path changes every public route below it, so clients, tests, documentation, and gateway rules must move together.
beats.recallRule: Class-level mapping supplies the shared route conditions; method-level mapping completes each endpoint.

sections.title: Class and method mappings are combined into final routes
sections.content:
`@RequestMapping` can appear on a controller type and on handler methods. At the class level it describes the common part of the controller's mapping. At the method level it narrows that mapping to one endpoint. Spring registers the resulting combination when the application starts.

Path composition is the easiest case. A controller path `/orders` plus a method path `/{id}` becomes `/orders/{id}`. A method with no additional path stays at `/orders`. The HTTP method still comes from `@GetMapping`, `@PostMapping`, or another method-specific mapping.

Shared media conditions can be helpful when every endpoint returns JSON. `produces = application/json` limits mapping by the client's acceptable response media type. A POST can also declare `consumes = application/json` to require a JSON request body.

Media conditions have a special rule: method-level `consumes` and `produces` override the class-level declarations rather than extending them. This lets one method deliberately accept or produce another format, but an accidental override can make a route behave differently from neighboring methods.

Spring warns when multiple request-mapping annotations are placed on the same class or method and uses only the first mapping it detects. Method-specific annotations should therefore stand alone on the method. A clean mapping tree improves organization, but authorization and backward compatibility still require separate design and tests.

sections.title: What belongs at each mapping level
sections.content:
| Mapping level | Good responsibility | Order example |
|---|---|---|
| Class `@RequestMapping` | Shared resource path | `/orders` |
| Method `@GetMapping` | Retrieval path and GET method | `/{id}` → `GET /orders/{id}` |
| Method `@PostMapping` | Creation route and request media type | empty path → `POST /orders` |
| Class media condition | Representation shared by every method | `produces = application/json` |
| Method media condition | A deliberate per-endpoint override | `consumes = application/json` on POST |
